intro: Anthropic just shattered IPO records with an $81.3 billion raise that briefly pushed the company toward a $2 trillion valuation — only to watch shares tumble the next day as a global AI sell-off reminded everyone that gravity still applies, even in the age of artificial intelligence. Beyond the market drama, today's digest is packed with colliding forces: Signal is locking its doors against AI agents reading your screen, Apple is building its own Mac-operating AI while quietly kneecapping the competition, and new research shows the people paying the highest cognitive price for the AI revolution are the ones who can least afford it. Buckle in — it's one of those days where the future feels like it's arriving faster than anyone planned for.

stories.title: Anthropic completes largest-ever IPO, shares whipsaw in first two days of trading
stories.summary: Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under ticker ANT at $83/share, raising $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX's record from five months prior. Shares opened at $111.50 and closed day one at $97.17 (up 17%), briefly valuing the company near $2 trillion. 96% of Anthropic's 5,000+ employees became paper millionaires, while early investors Amazon and Google saw their stakes reach $161 billion and $147 billion respectively. CEO Dario Amodei pledged that safety, not business or political pressure, would guide development pace. On day two, shares fell over 9% to $88.17 as a broader AI sector sell-off gripped global markets, with Asian markets recording their worst week since 2020 amid investor concerns about massive AI infrastructure spending.
stories.opinion: The whiplash from euphoric first-day gains to a sharp second-day sell-off captures the market's fundamental ambivalence about AI valuations — investors want in but remain skittish about the staggering capital requirements and unanswered profitability questions. Where coverage differs: The Rundown AI reports first-day closing price of $97.17 (up 17%); Guardian AI reports second-day price of $88.17 (down 9%), approaching the $83 IPO price — these are sequential days, not conflicting figures

stories.title: Analysts debate root causes of widespread tech outages as conspiracy theories swirl
stories.summary: A wave of major tech failures — including a multi-day Outlook outage, the second nationwide aviation ground stop in 25 years, banking disruptions, and iCloud downtime — prompted analysis from security experts and tech journalists. Bruce Schneier argues the outages are symptoms of shareholder capitalism driving underinvestment in reliable infrastructure, not coordinated cyberattacks. The Vergecast hosts found each incident was generally less severe than conspiracy theories suggested but argued the incidents collectively signal a worrying trend as AI replaces human oversight. The Vergecast episode also covered the ongoing Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal, noting it has shifted from personal affairs to allegations of illegal chip smuggling to China, with Huang unlikely to return as CEO.
stories.opinion: The consensus is these are not cyberattacks, but the disagreement over root cause — chronic underinvestment vs. premature AI automation — suggests these outages are symptoms of overlapping systemic problems, not a single fixable issue. Where coverage differs: Schneier attributes outages to shareholder capitalism and infrastructure underinvestment; The Verge frames the concern as AI replacing human oversight in critical systems

stories.title: Nvidia posts healthy earnings amid Huang scandal, halts H200 chip sales to China
stories.summary: Nvidia delivered its latest earnings report showing healthy growth despite ongoing fallout from the ouster of CEO Jensen Huang. The company announced it will stop selling H200 chips to China and dismissed calls to reinstate Huang. The TechCrunch Equity podcast also covered Waymo suspending national freeway rides, Tesla opening Cybercab personal orders with caveats, battery startup Our Next Energy going public, and Plural's new European moonshot fund.
stories.opinion: Nvidia's ability to post healthy growth without its iconic founder suggests the company's moat is deeper than any one leader, though the China chip halt adds a new strategic variable.

stories.title: Apple developing AI agent to operate Macs while restricting competing agents on macOS
stories.summary: Apple is developing an AI agent capable of browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services, based on a Bloomberg report and a now-removed job listing for a senior engineering manager. The agent would work with Apple's Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models teams. Apple has considered launching as soon as late 2027, but the project remains in early stages. Simultaneously, macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to competing agents from Anthropic (Duet), OpenAI (Dots), Meta (Muse), and Google (Tasks). The agent would emphasize privacy and Apple's signature polish.
stories.opinion: Apple's dual strategy of building its own agent while making it harder for competitors to operate on macOS is a familiar playbook — and one that will likely draw antitrust scrutiny given the precedent of recent app store battles. Where coverage differs: The Verge notes the job listing has been removed; TechCrunch does not mention this

stories.title: Russian national indicted for spying on Silicon Valley defense company employees on behalf of Moscow
stories.summary: Igor D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted for allegedly spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company (reported by Reuters and Bloomberg to be Palantir) on behalf of Russia. D'iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in summer 2026 after being recruited via Telegram, receiving instructions and funding to surveil company employees because the firm supplied weapons-related technology for use against Russian forces in Ukraine. His activities included photographing employees and their computer screens at a coffee shop near the company's Palo Alto office, compiling home addresses, and aggressively tailing a female employee for nearly 30 miles — an incident that ended only when she flagged a police patrol car.
stories.opinion: The case illustrates how traditional physical espionage is being directed at AI and defense tech companies, blending old-school surveillance tradecraft with the geopolitics of the Ukraine conflict.

stories.title: McClatchy pivots to AI-native newsroom as Pew data shows majority of Americans distrust AI in news
stories.summary: McClatchy, parent of the Miami Herald and Kansas City Star, is shifting to an 'AI-native operating model' after declaring its current business model unsustainable due to declining web traffic and subscribers. The move follows earlier staff cuts and has caused disputes with reporters. Pew Research data shows 56% of Americans say AI in news articles would decrease their confidence, Americans are five times more likely to predict negative than positive AI impact on news over 20 years, and 59% expect fewer journalism jobs.
stories.opinion: McClatchy's AI bet is a gamble against its own audience's stated preferences — most Americans say AI in news would make them trust it less, which makes the sustainability argument circular.

stories.title: AI adds hidden cognitive burden on lowest-paid workers, analysis argues
stories.summary: An analysis argues AI is imposing a hidden 'cognitive tax' on the lowest-paid workers, adding to the cognitive load of those already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing, and mounting debt. The piece calls for rethinking welfare systems for an AI-reshaped economy, noting that throughout economics history, the human brain — which directs labor, judgment, and resilience — has rarely been considered an asset worth protecting.
stories.opinion: Framing cognitive load as a regressive tax on workers least equipped to absorb it offers a useful policy lens for discussions that tend to focus narrowly on job displacement rather than the degradation of existing jobs.

stories.title: Pew survey finds broad satisfaction with 2026 midterm election administration
stories.summary: A Pew Research Center survey of 10,247 U.S. adults finds 83% of voters say elections across the country were run well, with 94% saying the same about their own community. Voters express more confidence in in-person than mail-in voting. The survey is part of a larger report on postelection attitudes following the Democrats' midterm victory, which found majority approval of the party's policies and plans.
stories.opinion: The high satisfaction numbers, especially at the local level, suggest election administration concerns are less salient to voters than political rhetoric implies.

stories.title: Six AI-powered gadgets for upgrading your home office
stories.summary: TechCrunch highlights six AI-powered home office gadgets: the Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159) for meeting transcription, Anker Soundcore Work ($159) recording pin with AI transcription, Logitech MX Keypad ($99) with AI assistant shortcuts for GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($629) with AI handwriting cleanup and note summarization, and Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249) AI-tracking webcam.
stories.opinion: The roundup shows AI assistant hardware maturing from novelty to practical productivity tools, with sub-$200 price points suggesting a mainstream consumer market is emerging.

stories.title: Signal blocks Gemini and Siri AI from reading users' screens by default
stories.summary: Signal is restricting screenshot capabilities on Android and iOS to prevent AI agents like Gemini and Siri from reading users' messages and on-screen data. Signal president Meredith Whittaker criticized OS-level agentic AI features as 'hostile to privacy' and urged Google, Apple, and Microsoft to provide better tools for app developers to control AI data access. Users can re-enable screenshots in Signal's settings, but the default will block them. Signal noted it cannot implement these protections on macOS due to insufficient developer controls from Apple.
stories.opinion: Signal's move highlights an emerging battleground between messaging privacy and OS-level AI agents — and the macOS gap suggests Apple's privacy reputation may not extend to giving developers the tools to enforce it.

tweet_headlines.author: undefinedKi
tweet_headlines.headline: Anthropic's __27-page Claude Code guide__ draws on real setups from Higgsfield, ClickHouse, and Harvey to show how top teams actually ship with AI.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Anthropic has a 27-page guide on how top startups ship their products

They talked to teams like Higgsfield, ClickHouse and Harvey, and they shared the actual Claude Code setups they use every day.

There are a lot of insights inside. Seven tips worth adding to your own workflow, even if you build alone:

1. If you keep pasting from a tool into Claude, connect that tool. And if it already has a good CLI, like gh or psql, let Claude use the CLI. It can cost fewer tokens than MCP

2. Split your instructions in three. Root CLAUDE.md for what can never change. A CLAUDE.md inside a folder for the conventions of that folder. Skills for procedures you only need sometimes

3. Use hooks for anything that must happen every time. A hook runs no matter what the model decides. Block a commit until the tests pass, or strip secrets before anything leaves the sandbox

4. Use /goal on long tasks. On those Claude can call the job done too early and drift from what you asked

5. Say "fan out multiple subagents". Claude splits a large analysis across parallel agents, or sends one agent to pick apart another agent's work

6. Start any rewrite in plan mode (Shift+Tab). Claude reads the codebase and proposes the approach before writing a line. It is the cheapest place to catch a bad direction

7. Rebuild in a git worktree. You get v2 running next to v1 and merge only when the new one wins

There is a one-page checklist at the end with the practical steps.

Here's the PDF

Sin cuenta.
Sin API key.
Sin internet.
Sin pagar tokens.

Configuración en 1 minuto:

1. sudo fm license (una vez, con tu contraseña)
2. fm available (comprueba que el modelo está)
3. fm respond “tu pregunta”

Funciona en cualquier Mac con Apple Silicon, incluido el M1.

human_items.headline: AI adds hidden cognitive burden on lowest-paid workers, analysis argues
human_items.summary: An analysis argues AI is imposing a hidden 'cognitive tax' on the lowest-paid workers, adding to the cognitive load of those already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing, and mounting debt. The piece calls for rethinking welfare systems for an AI-reshaped economy, noting that throughout economics history, the human brain — which directs labor, judgment, and resilience — has rarely been considered an asset worth protecting.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.

human_items.headline: Anthropic completes largest-ever IPO, shares whipsaw in first two days of trading
human_items.summary: Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under ticker ANT at $83/share, raising $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX's record from five months prior. Shares opened at $111.50 and closed day one at $97.17 (up 17%), briefly valuing the company near $2 trillion. 96% of Anthropic's 5,000+ employees became paper millionaires, while early investors Amazon and Google saw their stakes reach $161 billion and $147 billion respectively. CEO Dario Amodei pledged that safety, not business or political pressure, would guide development pace. On day two, shares fell over 9% to $88.17 as a broader AI sector sell-off gripped global markets, with Asian markets recording their worst week since 2020 amid investor concerns about massive AI infrastructure spending.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.

human_items.headline: Russian national indicted for spying on Silicon Valley defense company employees on behalf of Moscow
human_items.summary: Igor D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted for allegedly spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company (reported by Reuters and Bloomberg to be Palantir) on behalf of Russia. D'iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in summer 2026 after being recruited via Telegram, receiving instructions and funding to surveil company employees because the firm supplied weapons-related technology for use against Russian forces in Ukraine. His activities included photographing employees and their computer screens at a coffee shop near the company's Palo Alto office, compiling home addresses, and aggressively tailing a female employee for nearly 30 miles — an incident that ended only when she flagged a police patrol car.
